Subject: Redwood vs Hyperscaler — post-call recap & next steps

Hi Alicia,

Thanks again for the time today 026-08-01 . Quick recap and proposed next steps so we're all aligned:

- Scope: 10k qps bursty traffic for context-windowed summarization (avg prompt ~350 tokens, response target ~150 tokens).
- Goal: side-by-side A/B test to validate p95/p99 latency and sustained tokens/sec across your peak profile; verify quality parity on our eval set.
- Proposed tests (we discussed):
  1) Single-request latency (p50/p95/p99) at production input size.
  2) Sustained throughput test (tokens/sec) with continuous streams at target concurrency.
  3) Failure/fallback behavior under degraded capacity.

Action items we agreed on:
- Globex: share a sanitized eval prompt set + expected output checks (Ben to deliver by 8/3).
- Redwood: run A/B between our hosted endpoint (rwd-v2) and your hyperscaler endpoint using the same harness, return CSV with lat/throughput and a short analysis (I'll send by EOD 8/4).
- Follow-up: 30-min sync to review results and discuss model/quantization tradeoffs (propose 8/5 09:00 PT).

Attaching the proposed test harness config and the CSV template we'll populate.

Thanks 

Best,
Marissa Cole

Perfect we got the eval set. Quick note on methodology we'll use so results are interpretable:

- Harness: identical client harness hitting both endpoints (same concurrency, same prompt order, same seed).
- Sequence buckets: short (<=128 tokens) and long (avg 500 tokens).
- Measurements:
  * Latency to first token (TTFT) and latency to last token (TTL) per request.
  * p50/p95/p99 computed across 10k sample requests per bucket.
  * Sustained tokens/sec measured over 3 x 5-minute windows at target concurrency (to capture warm-cache steady state).
- Config: we'll test with and without server-side batching; quantized weights (int8) where supported.

We'll share raw CSV and a one-page summary ahead of the sync.

—Marissa
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
To: Alicia Gomez <alicia.gomez@globex.com>
Cc: Rafael Mendes <rafael@redwood.ai>, Jonas Weber <jonas@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-08-04T18:17:00-07:00
Subject: Redwood vs Hyperscaler — AB test results (summary + CSV)

Alicia / Ben  attaching results from the A/B run we completed earlier today. High-level summary first, then the CSV is attached.

Summary (short sequences <=128 tokens):
- Redwood (rwd-v2, int8 quantized, server batching off):
  * TTFT p50: 12 ms; p95: 38 ms; p99: 85 ms
  * TTL p50: 62 ms; p95: 145 ms; p99: 290 ms
  * Sustained tokens/sec (steady state): 2,800 tokens/sec

- Hyperscaler (hyp-std, baseline configuration, server batching default):
  * TTFT p50: 18 ms; p95: 72 ms; p99: 160 ms
  * TTL p50: 95 ms; p95: 220 ms; p99: 450 ms
  * Sustained tokens/sec: 1,900 tokens/sec

Summary (long sequences ~500 tokens):
- Redwood:
  * TTFT p50: 18 ms; p95: 55 ms; p99: 120 ms
  * TTL p50: 420 ms; p95: 890 ms; p99: 1,700 ms
  * Sustained tokens/sec: 2,450 tokens/sec

- Hyperscaler:
  * TTFT p50: 26 ms; p95: 110 ms; p99: 260 ms
  * TTL p50: 580 ms; p95: 1,200 ms; p99: 2,500 ms
  * Sustained tokens/sec: 1,650 tokens/sec

Key takeaways:
- Redwood demonstrates ~40-50% higher sustained tokens/sec across both buckets using the same model family; p95/p99 latency also materially lower, especially for TTL under load.
- Differences are most pronounced at high concurrency / long sequences  our KV/cache and continuous-batching optimizations reduce tail latency.
- Quality: final-output similarity between runs (BLEU/ROUGE-like checks on your eval set) is within the expected tolerance; no regressions observed. Full metric table is in the CSV.

Attachments: redwood_abtest_results.csv, redwood_batching_deepdive.pdf

Next steps I propose for the sync:
- Walk through the CSV and clarifying questions.
- Discuss options to reduce hyperscaler tail latency (e.g., tuned batching, pre-WARM strategies) vs. Redwood routing options (dedicated capacity, pinning, quantization profiles).
- Outline procurement/po timeline if you want to pilot Dedicated capacity.

Can we keep the 8/5 09:00 PT slot? I'll include Rafael (solutions eng) and Jonas (bench lead) to walk through the details.

Best,
Marissa

Marissa,

Thanks for the detailed write-up  the numbers look promising. Quick question ahead of the sync: can you confirm whether the sustained tokens/sec figures are measured with network latency emulated (we have 20-30 ms cross-region) or on the same region? Also, can you surface the batch sizes you tested for server-side batching?

If you can put that info in the CSV or a single slide, that would help our infra folks. See you at 09:00 PT.

Ben
From: Rafael Mendes <rafael@redwood.ai>
To: Ben Chu <ben.chu@globex.com>, Alicia Gomez <alicia.gomez@globex.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>, Jonas Weber <jonas@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-08-06T10:22:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Redwood vs Hyperscaler — AB test results (summary + CSV)

Ben  good questions. Short answers below and I'll walk through in the sync:

- Network: tests were run in us-west-2 for both endpoints (no additional cross-region latency emulation). We've included a column in the CSV with raw RTT per request so you can rebaseline for your 20-30 ms cross-region.
- Batching: baseline runs listed above were with server-side batching OFF for Redwood; we also ran a parallel set with batching ON (batch sizes 8/16/32 depending on concurrency)  those rows are labelled batch_on_* in the CSV. Hyperscaler runs used their default batching pipeline (they were effectively batching at ~16 on average).
- Quantization: Redwood runs used int8 in these tests; we also have fp16 runs available if you want a quality vs perf comparison.

I'll share a quick slide in the meeting that highlights the batch_on rows vs batch_off so infra can see the tradeoffs.

Rafael
Solutions Engineering, Redwood Inference
